name: Cobalamin A/B defect (vitamin B12-responsive methylmalonic acidaemia)

reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorders of intramitochondrial adenosylcobalamin synthesis (cblA due to MMAA, cblB due to MMAB) that impair methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, causing isolated methylmalonic acidaemia
They are the classic vitamin B12-responsive forms of methylmalonic acidaemia, and the cblA subtype in particular often responds well to hydroxocobalamin
Present with metabolic acidosis, hyperammonaemia, vomiting, lethargy and failure to thrive, typically precipitated by protein load or catabolic illness
Because adenosylcobalamin (not methylcobalamin) synthesis is affected, homocysteine is normal, distinguishing these from the combined cblC/cblD defects
Urine organic acids show markedly elevated methylmalonic acid; blood acylcarnitines show raised propionylcarnitine (C3)
A cobalamin-responsiveness trial with hydroxocobalamin is a key part of assessment, alongside protein restriction and carnitine supplementation

Management combines vitamin B12 (hydroxocobalamin) for responsive patients, avoidance of fasting and protein moderation, an emergency regimen with glucose during illness, and treatment of hyperammonaemia during crises
reference.pathophysiology: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase requires adenosylcobalamin as its cofactor to convert methylmalonyl-CoA to succinyl-CoA in the pathway that handles propiogenic substrates (certain amino acids, odd-chain fatty acids and cholesterol side-chains). The cblA (MMAA) and cblB (MMAB) defects impair the mitochondrial synthesis and delivery of adenosylcobalamin, so mutase activity is reduced despite a structurally normal enzyme. Methylmalonyl-CoA and its derivative methylmalonic acid accumulate, and propionyl-CoA is diverted to propionylcarnitine and related metabolites; secondary inhibition of the urea cycle contributes to hyperammonaemia during decompensation. Because only adenosylcobalamin is affected, methionine synthase activity and homocysteine remain normal. Provision of pharmacological hydroxocobalamin can restore cofactor supply in responsive patients, particularly the cblA type.
additionalDifferentials: Methylmalonic acidaemia from methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (mut) deficiency
Combined methylmalonic acidaemia and homocystinuria (cblC/cblD defects)
Dietary or maternal vitamin B12 deficiency
Transcobalamin and intrinsic-factor cobalamin transport defects
additionalInvestigations: Urine organic acids demonstrating markedly elevated methylmalonic acid
Plasma acylcarnitine profile showing raised propionylcarnitine (C3)
Plasma total homocysteine (normal here, distinguishing from cblC/cblD)
Blood gas, ammonia, glucose and lactate during acute presentations
Complementation studies and MMAA/MMAB molecular genetic testing to define the subtype
redFlags: Severe metabolic acidosis with hyperammonaemia and encephalopathy during a crisis
Recurrent vomiting, lethargy and poor feeding with failure to thrive
Rapid deterioration triggered by protein load or intercurrent illness
Evolving renal impairment, a recognised long-term complication of methylmalonic acidaemia
reference.prognosis: The cobalamin-responsive forms, especially cblA, generally have a better prognosis than mutase-deficient methylmalonic acidaemia, and many respond well to hydroxocobalamin with dietary management; nonetheless, poorly controlled disease carries risks of neurological injury and progressive renal impairment.
pitfalls: Not performing a formal cobalamin-responsiveness trial and missing a treatable form
Failing to measure homocysteine and thereby confusing these defects with combined cblC/cblD disease
Overlooking hyperammonaemia and secondary carnitine deficiency during crises
Neglecting long-term monitoring of renal function
references: Scriver's OMMBID: Disorders of Cobalamin Metabolism and Methylmalonic Acidaemia
Saudubray, Baumgartner & Walter, Inborn Metabolic Diseases: Diagnosis and Treatment
management: Pharmacological hydroxocobalamin as the disease-specific therapy, to which cobalamin-responsive forms, especially cblA, respond well.
Dietary restriction of propiogenic protein with a specialised methylmalonic acidaemia formula to limit substrate load.
L-carnitine supplementation to promote excretion of accumulated propionyl groups and prevent secondary carnitine depletion.
An emergency sick-day regimen during intercurrent illness, reversing catabolism with high-energy glucose feeds and reduced protein intake.
Aggressive management of acute metabolic decompensation, correcting metabolic acidosis and treating hyperammonaemia with nitrogen-scavenging drugs and, if severe, haemofiltration or dialysis.
Long-term monitoring of methylmalonic acid, acylcarnitines, growth and renal function, with surveillance for chronic renal impairment.
Multidisciplinary metabolic care with a specialist dietitian, and genetic counselling for these autosomal recessive MMAA and MMAB disorders.
